title: Models, context windows, tokens and limits

items.scenario: In one afternoon you must (a) risk-review an 80-page vendor master services agreement and (b) make a release announcement sound friendlier.
items.question: Which model and effort plan is most appropriate?
options: Use the most capable model at maximum effort for both, to be safe
Use the default model and effort for both; choosing per task is premature optimisation
Contract review on a strong model at high effort with the document first and questions last; the rewrite on a faster model at low effort
Use the fastest model for the contract since it's long, and the strongest model for the announcement since it's customer-facing
items.explanation: Match model and effort to the task: long-document reasoning benefits from a capable model and higher effort; a tone rewrite is a light language task where speed and usage matter more.
distractors: Max effort on a rewrite burns time and usage with no quality gain.
Defaults over-pay on easy tasks and can under-think hard ones; the objective is choosing deliberately.
Inverted: document length calls for capability and careful reasoning, not the fastest model.

items.scenario: Your team is about to hard-code a model ID into a nightly ticket-classification job and the team's prompt guide.
items.question: What should you do before standardising on that model?
options: Check the model deprecation page and record the model's retirement status and date where it's pinned
Nothing — models are supported indefinitely once released
Pick the oldest available model because it's the most stable
Ask Claude which models will be retired soon
items.explanation: Models are deprecated and then retired; a pinned job fails at retirement. The deprecation page is the authoritative source to check before standardising.
distractors: Models do retire; retired models stop answering requests.
Older models are closer to retirement, not further from it.
The model's training cut-off means it may not know current deprecation plans; check the official page.

items.scenario: A teammate wants to zip a 150,000-line monorepo and paste it into a chat to ask architecture questions.
items.question: What's the best response?
options: Go ahead — the current context window is large enough for any repository
Paste only the README; that's enough for architecture questions
Split the repo into ten chats and paste a tenth into each
Estimate first (roughly 10 tokens per line ≈ 1.5M tokens, which doesn't fit) and use Claude Code to explore the repo agentically instead
items.explanation: Code is token-dense; a large repo exceeds the context window, and stuffing is slow, costly and less accurate. Claude Code searches and reads only relevant files.
distractors: Large context windows still have a limit, and quality degrades when relevant facts are buried in huge contexts.
A README rarely reflects the real architecture; Claude needs the relevant code.
Chats share no state, so no single chat can reason across the whole system.

items.scenario: You need an accurate token budget for a prompt template before shipping a feature on the API. A colleague suggests using tiktoken because it's already installed.
items.question: How should you count tokens?
options: tiktoken is fine — all modern models share the same tokenizer
Use the API's count_tokens endpoint with the same model ID you'll use in production
Count words and multiply by 1.3; that's exact for code too
Count characters and divide by 4 for every content type
items.explanation: Token counts are model-specific and tokenizers change between generations. Count with the target model's own tokenizer; rough ratios are for estimates only.
distractors: Tokenizers differ between vendors and between Claude generations; tiktoken undercounts Claude tokens.
~1.3 tokens/word is a rough English-prose heuristic; code and non-English text are much denser.
Chars/4 is a prose estimate, not a budget; it breaks for code, JSON and non-English.

items.scenario: Claude tells you confidently that 'the latest version' of a popular web framework is a specific number and recommends an API from it. It cites nothing.
items.question: What's the right move?
options: Trust it — the model was trained on the framework's documentation
Ask the same question again; if the answer repeats, it's correct
Treat it as possibly stale (training cut-off) and force a web search with citations, then verify against the official docs
Switch to the highest effort level, which gives the model access to current information
items.explanation: 'Latest' facts after the training cut-off are unknown to the model, which won't know it's stale. Force a search and check sources.
distractors: Training data stops at the cut-off; later releases are invisible to the model.
Repetition shows consistency, not correctness.
Effort controls reasoning depth, not access to live information.

items.scenario: A CI test for your LLM-powered summariser asserts the exact output string for a fixed input. It fails about one run in five.
items.question: What's the best fix?
options: Assert properties (required fields present, valid JSON, length bounds) and track the pass rate on a small eval set
Retry the test until it passes
Lower the effort to minimum so output is deterministic
Delete the test; LLM features can't be tested
items.explanation: Outputs are non-deterministic by design. Test properties across a set of inputs and judge the distribution, not one golden string.
distractors: Retry-until-green hides real failure rates.
Lower effort doesn't make sampling deterministic.
LLM features are testable — with property assertions and eval sets.

items.scenario: Mid-way through a release-day migration, you hit your 5-hour usage limit on your company seat.
items.question: Which response is appropriate?
options: Continue the work on your personal account until the window resets
Ask a colleague for their login
Paste everything into a free chatbot from another vendor
Switch to a lighter model or lower effort where the task allows, use credits if your plan and policy permit, or queue work for the next window
items.explanation: Work within limits using model/effort choice, sanctioned credits, or planning; never move company data to personal or unapproved tools.
distractors: Moves company data outside org governance — an M8.1 violation.
Credential sharing breaches policy and the audit trail.
Unapproved tools are an uncontrolled data disclosure.

items.scenario: Your manager asks why the weekly status summaries changed in length and style this week, though the prompt is unchanged.
items.question: What's the most likely explanation to investigate first?
options: Claude remembered last week's feedback from other users
The model or effort level changed (new default, someone's switch, or a retirement), compounded by normal output variation
The prompt got corrupted in transit
Claude is learning from your team's chats in real time
items.explanation: Different models and effort levels behave differently, and outputs vary run to run. Check what changed, re-validate, and pin the choice.
distractors: There's no cross-user memory; each chat starts fresh except for your own memory/Projects.
Possible but unlikely; model/effort changes are the common cause.
Models don't update from your conversations in real time.

items.scenario: You ran the same hard debugging task at Low, High and Max effort. High and Max gave equally correct root causes; Max took three times longer.
items.question: What should your team guide recommend for this task type?
options: Max, because more effort is always better
Low, because it was fastest
High as the default, escalating to higher effort only when High is shown to fall short
Alternate effort levels randomly to average out non-determinism
items.explanation: Extra effort has diminishing returns. Use the lowest level that reliably succeeds and escalate on evidence — the point of the effort-ladder exercise.
distractors: Past the point where quality stops improving, more effort only costs time and usage.
Low didn't solve the task correctly in this scenario — speed without correctness is waste.
Randomising adds variance and tells you nothing.

items.scenario: You paste a 900-page specification into a chat and ask a question whose answer is a single clause on page 430. The answer misses it.
items.question: Which change most improves the result?
options: Add the full specification twice so the clause appears more often
Narrow the context to the relevant sections, put the document before the question, and ask for the quote with its location
Ask in a new chat without the document; the model already knows the spec
Raise effort to Max and keep the full document — context size doesn't affect accuracy
items.explanation: Long contexts cost more and models can under-use facts buried in the middle. Relevant, well-placed context and quote-grounding beat sheer volume.
distractors: Doubling the context doubles cost and noise; it doesn't fix retrieval.
Without the document, the model can only guess or hallucinate the clause.
Context size and placement do affect accuracy; effort alone won't fix a buried fact.
